findings.description: Packaging can still report `published` after `pack` dirties the repository, so the release record can point at a tree that is no longer the tree that was verified.
findings.failureScenario: A repository adopts the documented packaging hook and uses a normal pack command or wrapper that writes the package artifact to `{output}` **and** emits intermediates under the repo. The shipped examples point operators at `dotnet pack -o {output}`, and build commands like that commonly leave side files outside the final package directory. On the current implementation, `package()` snapshots `tree_digest` before `pack`, never checks the worktree again, and still returns `published` as long as an artifact appears in `{output}` and `push` exits 0. That means the feed can receive artifacts from a tree that no longer matches the verified clean tree, and the later close can fail `working_tree_clean`. Because packaging is expressly built around repo-defined build commands, this is a probable main-path failure, not a contrived edge.

findings.description: **Nit:** `package(set_dir, config=None)` calls `load_config()` without `project_dir`, so an explicit `--session-set-dir` only picks up the target repo's `local-overrides.yaml` when the current working directory is already that repo (`ai_router/packaging.py`, `ai_router/config.py`).

findings.description: `ai_router/packaging.py`’s `_moved_the_tree()` is not quite the same fail-closed rule that `ai_router/checks.py` uses: if the post-command snapshot returns `None`, `_moved_the_tree()` also returns `None`, so a snapshot failure is indistinguishable from “tree unchanged”.

The human-facing message in `ai_router/packaging.py` / `docs/schema-reference.md` says that on tree mutation “nothing was pushed”, but mutation is only checked *after* each `push` command returns; a push implementation that uploads first and dirties the repo second would still end `failed` after an artifact had already been published.
